articles.title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion
articles.content: Posted by mame on 18 Nov 2026 Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading. CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 : Heap buffer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x : Double free in regular expression compilation Ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px : Integer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive regular expression matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way. GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w : Heap buffer overflow in regular expression compilation Ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. Ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s . Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive backreference matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process. Affected versions Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12 Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9 Recommended action We strongly recommend upgradin

articles.title: The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026
articles.content: The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026. The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines. 'Human' is defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as ‘having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines’. In 2026, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a widely read essay . Commenting on the selection of ‘human’ as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, he said: “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human. It could help us cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most. "But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.” ‘AI godfather’ and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has warned that “we’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans.” And in his Magnifica Humanitas letter, Pope Leo XIV spoke of new forms of “dehumanization” and the “pressing duty to remain profoundly human”. Actors Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, musicians Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes and Billie Eilish, and authors Jodi Picoult and Jonathan Franzen challenged an "assault on human creativity" as the Human Artistry Campaign and Artist Rights Alliance opposed machine-generated replicas and theft of human-generated content by large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir has wondered whether he "might be among the last generation of fully human writers". The Authors Guild has launched a ‘Human Authored’ kitemark for books, supported by Professor Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman. As AI deepfakes simulated humans, Matthew McConaughey became the first Hollywood actor to pre-emptively protect himself against unauthorised digital reproduction by trademarking clips of his voice, his face and even his catchphrase ‘alright, alright, alright’. Taylor Swift followed suit, trademarking her voice and image in April. Professor Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common. “AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There’s a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them." articles.title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
articles.content: Executive Summary Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs. NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server , it powers more than 225 million websites . Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released. We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes. Responsible disclosure timeline October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability. November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review. November 16, 2026 : Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5. November 17, 2026 : F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release. November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure. Overview Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules. Wiz Resea
articles.summary: 多家安全机构独立发现 NGINX 两个未授权远程代码执行漏洞，影响大量生产应用与 API 入口。

articles.title: Gemini 4 Neon looks like an Opus 5.5 competitor
articles.content: TLDR: we project Gemini 4 Neon’s performance based on what a faster Gemini 4 Carbon might score and find it equivalent to Opus 5.5 Gemini 4 Carbon is the best model on the Agent Duel leaderboard if you exclude early voting. Carbon’s main problem is that it is slooooow . Today, Gemini 4 Neon was released , and looks to be an incremental benchmark improvement with a very large speed improvement. Earlier today, it was being served extremely fast via OpenRouter: 127 tokens per second . This is way faster than Carbon at 46 tokens per second . This got me wondering, could Neon be not just a good model but the best model? Modeling our leaderboard To investigate, I modeled the win rate in our leaderboard. The best model has three components, model identity, speed and whether the user voted early. My initial modeling did poorly, so I added an interaction between speed and early voting. This ended up working well. And surprisingly, speed seems to be pretty much as important as model identity (another blog on that soon). Projecting Gemini 4 Neon performance If you assume the same performance as Gemini 4 Carbon (which is reasonable given even better benchmark scores), and 127 tps , we would project an Elo on the Agent Duel leaderboard of 1,066, just below Opus 5.5 at 1,078 in our later analysis snapshot. The 90% interval for the projected Elo difference between Gemini 4 Neon and Opus 5.5 is -94 to +68, with Neon projected to win 48.3% of the time against Opus (counting ties as half a win).

articles.title: AI agents ask better questions than KPMG accountants in audit trial
articles.content: LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team. The experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an important development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how quickly will the economics of auditing change? According to the Financial Times , the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions. Join The European Business Briefing New subscribers this quarter are entered into a draw to win a Rolex Submariner. Join 40,000+ founders, investors and executives who read EBM every day. KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into issues than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised. The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged. From supporting accountants to conducting audits Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow. The agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation. The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the company’s accounts. Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks. articles.title: LLM assisted reverse engineering
articles.content: I have been hacking both hardware and software for 2 decades. Previously manually. But in 2026 with the help of AIs the proccess is greatly sped up. Below I will describe my proccess briefly or how I do it. Set Up Tools which I mostly use are these: Process What I basically do nowadays is just point the agent at the binary to be analysed and use my set of dedicated agent skills. Rest usually takes care of itself. But putting the skills besides, the flow is basically this. Find binary type, platform, build etc - based on this using appropriate decompiler (note - current AIs do fairly well with just disassembly . ie pure x86 or ARM instructions). Command agent to document all findings along the way to MD files. This serves several purposes. They become notes for your own understanding. They help the agent not lose the track after compaction / handoff to different agent. And last but not least, it helps the agent work more effectively, not get lost in circles etc. More about this later. Ask the agent to analyse basic structure. Main functions, main branching, imported functions etc of given binary. By binary I mean whatever. Desktop executable, website or firmware image. Once I have this basic overview I can usually proceed any way I need to do modifications to the original binary or build mods or just help me understand it better. On some occasions some things are not easily resolvable by simple disassembly or decompilation. In those cases you can do: Let the agent debug given binary and set breakpoints on specific parts to help it figure out given inner workings. Use logging. Either by somehow enabling it in the original binary or by making a probe (and this can mean many things) that injects to the original binary and records you via logs (to file) whatever is needed to resolve given feature. Give agent outside access - ie computer use for desktop apps, or api controllable emulator for running and controlling given firmware. Ask agent to try different approach. But you must be specific. Ie when it gets stuck in disasembly by following xrefs, ask it to try to follow strings in the binary instead. Read the entire LLM conversation and thinking. Current LLMs are smart but they still sometimes get to a narrow approach. By reading the traces you can often instinctively figure the agent it going into a blind path and give it suggestion as to how it might be approached better. That however skill of your own to have. SKILLS Here are some of my major skills I use frequently. Matt Pottock - Grill me It gives you several questions when your input might be valuable. I usually use it with this prompt: text Use skill /grill-me to ask me up to 5 questions whose answers are crucial for your further progress. Ask only one question at a time. mattpocock / skills Shell Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab. articles.title: DNS resolvers are the wrong place to fight piracy
articles.content: On Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of users. It is leaving because a Paris court fined it for refusing to block a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around 20 similar cases still pending in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford. Cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure "a canary in the coal mine" , and the post reached the front page of Hacker News . In that thread, Quad9's CTO John Todd asked readers to write "a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path", with plenty of sources, and to send it to policymakers. This is our attempt. Every claim below links to a primary document, a court ruling, or contemporaneous reporting. What Quad9 is, and why it matters ​ A DNS resolver turns a name like example.com into an IP address your computer can connect to. Most people use their ISP's resolver without knowing it. A public resolver is one anyone can point their device or network at instead, such as Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Cisco's OpenDNS, or Quad9's 9.9.9.9. Quad9 has a few properties that make it unusual: Organisations have come to depend on it. Mullvad shut down its own public encrypted DNS service on November 2, 2026 and moved Mullvad Browser users with default settings to Quad9, funding Quad9 instead. (Mullvad Browser users in France will now be migrated to a resolver that disappears three weeks later.) Quad9's announcement lists dozens of French networks it sees traffic from, including the interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP-HM hospitals in Marseille, France Télévisions, Thales, and Airbus's Stormshield . Quad9 can't tell any of them it is leaving. As Cloudflare points out , when a resolver disappears, users don't see an error message. "Their Internet will simply stop working." How France got here ​ The law: Article L.333-10 of the Code du sport ​ The legal basis for all of this is Article L.333-10 of the French sports code . It was created by Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021 , the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the new regulator Arcom . L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer à y remédier" (any person able to help stop the infringement). That last phrase is what puts DNS resolvers in scope. In July 2026 , Parliament passed Law 2026-725 on professional sport , which amended L.333-10 and added an automated real-time blocking system run by Arcom. TorrentFreak reported that under the new system "ARCOM

articles.title: nginx2root
articles.content: Introduction nginx is one of the most widely deployed web servers in the world. Finding an unauthenticated remote code execution bug in it has long been a holy grail for security researchers. The Xint research team recently found five. Each one leads to remote code execution on its own, but they affect different configurations. Xint also found a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel which can be chained with any of the nginx vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. Together, we call these six vulnerabilities nginx2root . If you run nginx, update to 1.31.9 as soon as the fixed release becomes available. This article explains the root cause of each nginx2root vulnerability and summarizes our exploitability assessments. For exposure checks, see Section 2 and for patching and temporary mitigations, see Section 3. 1. Executive Summary What an attacker can do The most impactful of the five findings, CVE-2026-123007, allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The commands run with the privileges of the nginx worker process that handles the request. We chained this vulnerability with a separate flaw in the Linux kernel's SCTP subsystem to gain root privileges on the host. In our tests, the chain also escaped a Docker container running nginx and obtained root on the underlying host. In the video below, we use CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the nginx worker inside a container, then use the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host. nginx2root demo video We ran this demo on AWS, attacking the server over its public IP address. Demos for AWS, GCP, Azure, and bare-metal servers are available at nginx2root.com . Affected versions Each one of the five nginx vulnerabilities are independent attack paths and do not need to be chained together. They differ in what configuration is affected. CVE Affected configuration First affected release for this path Blocked by disabling HTTP/2? CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 enabled 1.9.5 Yes CVE-2026-123634 resolver , a request-derived proxy_pass destination, and mirror with mirror_request_body off 1.13.4 No CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2 with requests forwarded to an upstream (backend) server 1.19.7 Yes CVE-2026-121810 HTTP/3 with requests forwarded to an upstream (backend) server 1.25.0 No CVE-2026-113425 Mail proxy using proxy on and auth_http 0.5.15 No For CVE-2026-123634, the table shows the setup we tested, which uses the mirror directive. articles.title: Windows 11 collects data on which coding agents and dev tools you use
articles.content: Reverse engineering Windows 11's MissionControlAggregator reveals coding-agent and developer-tool usage bits in a diagnostic ETW report. I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe , claude.exe , copilot.exe , and cursor.exe , alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe , dotnet.exe , gcc.exe , and code.exe . Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools? The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll . I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft. I shared the initial finding on X . This post includes more details about the investigation behind it. Following the names Opening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component: Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe , claude.exe , codex.exe , and agy.exe , with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe , claude.exe , codex.exe , cursor.exe , and antigravity.exe . Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe : The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers . For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call . The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison. The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage , feature ID 62580080 . And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe , python.exe , dotnet.exe , gcc.exe , clang.exe , gdb.exe , javac.exe , devenv.exe , and code.exe , among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation , Python expects Python Software Foundation , and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation . The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path. Where does the DLL get this information? articles.title: Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere
articles.content: The Tail of Base64 By Quang Luong On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution. Discovery A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode. Lesson learned Complicated system interactions are hard, and this complexity can make exploiting hard bugs easy. After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway. Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues. Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder... Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold? Note That sheer persistence is prompting AI and ignoring slops for around 20 minutes, by the way. The vulnerability The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub , the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are

articles.title: Actual curl rewrites in rust
articles.content: For a long time we have received repeated requests for, or questions about, a curl rewrite in rust. Often as a joke, but also seriously. A joke from years ago In this modern world of AIs, we have only been waiting for someone to prove it possible and now it seems we don’t have to wait anymore. This fall seems to be the time of the curl-in-rust takes as we first saw urlx appear a few months ago, claimed to be a memory-safe, from-scratch reimplementation of curl and libcurl and now in November curl, rewritten in Rust – a rewrite of curl and libcurl in Rust . This second one confusingly enough not even using a different name. This latter one claims to have spent 8,600 USD to make it happen. Writing code once was never the issue Writing code once was never the big deal with software and it still isn’t. Sure, it’s fascinating that you can make a set of agents accomplish this in only a few weeks but let’s face it: it could do this because all the AIs of the world have trained on curl code for years. curl is extremely well documented, there are hundreds of existing open source application using its API and there are thousands of test cases to verify the implementation. The C code sits there and all the AI needs to do is convert it to rust, then polish until the tests work. A know-it-all person’s comment from years ago curl is the result of time curl has come to be what it is thanks to many decisions, lots of time, many users, oceans of feedback and many iterations. Sure, recreating what curl is at any specific single moment in time is certainly doable. Doable, because we have made a perfect specification for that project. Behind already During the time these agents converted 185,000 lines of C code into 340,000 lines of Rust code (I counted), we merged over 300 commits in the actual curl project. We actually improved curl during these a little more than three weeks. A little over 200 bugfixes actually. 200 bugfixes that none of those rust rewrites have. We also fixed a few vulnerabilities. In another month we have done another 200 and maybe fixed a few more vulnerabilities. Will these clones keep up? The constant tweaking, fixing, improving and extending is what makes a software project live, what makes it attractive to users and what makes it able to compete with alternatives. That fixing, and occasional new feature, is a direct result of a working community of users, contributors and maintainers. That goes way beyond the source code or which language that is used. A primary reason it is hard to make a competing curl alternative is because of the development speed, the development team and the community around curl. It is not because of the chosen language it is implemented in. Only curl can boast decades of ABI and API stability and prove that we know this and can do it well – over time. An alternative that pops up today might be able to do it as well, and in a few decades we will know if they could . C I know I’m repeating myself but: out of the 81 v

articles.title: FreeBSD GUS
articles.content: RCU's cool cousin Introduction FreeBSD has a pretty neat safe memory reclamation scheme (something akin to RCU), that's also been adopted by XNU that hasn't really been well-documented outside of code comments, and I thought it would've been interesting to write about it. What safe memory reclamation is all about The problem of safe memory reclamation (SMR) shows up notably when working with lock-free data structures. Lock-free data structures are the bread and butter of modern scalability in operating systems, and they often allow much higher throughput than their finely grained locked counterparts, but they come with their own issues. Lock-free data structure code in unmanaged languages needs to carefully manage the liveness of the objects it manages, i.e it must guarantee that memory is freed if and only if no one is able to access it. This arises because there is no synchronization around the access of the data structure, so an object that is removed can still be visible concurrently by another CPU (who might have made a local copy). More broadly, SMR schemes can also be used for other things than memory reclamation, I like to think of them as providing barriers ensuring that all participants (read: CPUs or threads) have passed through a certain point. Prior art SMR schemes broadly fall in two families: Epoch-based reclamation (EBR) and Quiescent-state based reclamation (QSBR). You might have also heard of Hazard Pointers (HP), which are useful on their own but are seldom seen in operating systems (at least, that I know of!). QSBR is notable because you might've heard of it called a different name by the Linux project, RCU (Read-Copy-Update)! RCU's author, Paul McKenney, actually invented QSBR for the DYNIX operating system. RCU has been described extensively, and I would recommend reading McKenney's excellent LWN Articles to learn more. The TL;DR is that there are three operations: rcu_read_lock , rcu_read_unlock and rcu_synchronize , the read operations are used to guard reads around potentially-freed memory (i.e to enter a read section ) and the synchronize function waits until there is no CPU in a read section (this could be used to wait until memory is safe to be freed). The gist of the algorithm is that memory is known to be safe to free when all CPUs have gone through at least one quiescent point ever since the object was removed from its data structure (a grace period ), and read section operations block those quiescent points from ever happening. In practice, this can be implemented by having a quiescent point on context switches and inhibiting preemption during read operations. The core of the algorithm is actually pretty simple, and much of the complexity of the Linux code stems from making this scalable (Tree RCU) and handling other RCU flavors (e.g preemptible RCU). FreeBSD's safe memory reclamation scheme is called GUS and is part of the EBR family. Epoch-based reclamation Epoch-based reclamation was first described by Keir Fras
articles.summary: 文章介绍 FreeBSD 类似 RCU 的安全内存回收机制 GUS，该方案也被 XNU 采用。

articles.title: Java4Shell is a reason to use Java
articles.content: by: Ethan McCue Good Morning. We're less than a day into dealing with "Java4Shell" , an issue stemming from how the Java Virtual Machine intrinsifies Base64 encoding code. If you have a Java deployment you haven't updated yet, add -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to the VM flags. Then upgrade your VM to a version where the issue is patched when you can. This is just one in a string of high profile outages and vulnerabilities. AI is a good fuzzer, people are finding latent problems with much lower effort than the past. People are pretty worried about this because we're all pretty sure there are more latent problems to find. Vulnerabilities tend to be bigger problems when they stem from native code, and they tend to be widespread problems when they come from dependencies many people share. Java4Shell is both of these things. A lot of people use Java and the problem stems from a handwritten assembly intrinsic. Fun times. But, for a moment, lets say we trust the VM. It is a big dependency, but it is only one dependency. We can all agree to audit it more closely, reduce the amount of native code in it, proactively run AIs against it, etc. Of course. Normal Java programs are memory safe. If you use a library which wants to call native code you will get a warning, later a hard error , unless you the person using the library adds --enable-native-access=the.specific.library to their command-line options. This means even with a sprawling dependency tree, which is a problem for all programming language ecosystems, you can know your exact exposure to native code and what dependencies you need to audit more closely. Compare that to C#, which lets any dependency write assembly inline . Python, JavaScript, Go - everything speaks C and lets any one of your dependencies bring along native code. As we are all learning the hard way, this carries risk. Not only are Java programs memory safe. They are also fast. The exact mechanism which caused Java4Shell (the ability for the VM to swap out normal Java code for native code) combined with JIT compilation can make the actual performance of a Java program competitive with C. Sometimes a Java program can even be faster. A JIT compiler knows what code paths are actually taken and can optimize around them. They can even refocus what is optimized if the workload changes. It is pretty cool! Somewhat recently I went through the raytracing in a weekend book with Java. Impl mean ± σ vs C++ ───────────────────────────────────────────────── C++ clang 21 -O3 7.00 ±0.01 1.00x Java 28, value classes 11.95 ±0.25 1.71x C# .NET 11 preview 6 11.95 ±0.22 1.71x C# .NET 10 11.98 ±0.11 1.71x Java 26 17.53 ±0.21 2.50x Benchmarks can be problematic, I know. What I want you to take away is that the JVM makes your code fast enough that most people don't need native code. Unlike, to take a potshot, CPython. There everything is slow as molasses unless you make it a native extension. So if you are worried AI is going to find security problems with your co
articles.summary: Java 虚拟机 Base64 内联优化引发 Java4Shell 漏洞，作者建议未升级用户先加 -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics 参数并尽快升级 JVM。

articles.title: How I made a custom game engine for Satelital
articles.content: Seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch. And Last week I released Satelital, a rule-discovery game about learning alien logic. As a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch. My motivation was to learn the actual fundamentals behind the technology of videogames. This meant I had to build most of the tools I would need myself, including the game engine, renderer, puzzles, editors, UX, design, art and music. Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it. VIDEO The main reason I got into programming was the idea of eventually working on games. I spent many years working on web and building mobile apps. It was fun, but I felt like I wasn't going in the direction I really wanted to. So one day, after listening to every Jonathan Blow talk I could find and playing too much The Witness, I decided to finally give it a try. I spent many days and countless hours looking for the best tool I could use to make a game, but nothing left me satisfied. The closest I got to having fun with gamedev was with the LÖVE framework making a few jam games. But even with that, it felt quite limiting to not really know what was happening behind the graphics I somehow managed to animate on my screen. Early prototype of a tile-based level editor built with LÖVE and Lua. I remember hearing about shaders and parallel programming. The concept always felt very arcane and mysterious to me, but now writing them is the thing I enjoy the most while coding. I finally decided to jump into the swimming pool and actually learn C⁠+⁠+. I had to learn how to manage memory and how not to shoot myself in the foot with the wrong tools. I started using SDL2 while trying to use the C⁠+⁠+ standard library as little as possible. Before getting too deep into the engine, I actually finished a prototype of the puzzles not long after learning how to draw some simple graphics with C⁠+⁠+. It had very early versions of four kinds of puzzles that mostly survived until the final game. It was made entirely with SDL2, but I soon realised that if I wanted more interesting graphics, I would need to use shaders and decided to switch to OpenGL. Early prototype gameplay with SDL2 This puzzle was the first one I made, also the only one that survived until the end With the help of LearnOpenGL I quickly had a triangle on the screen. From there, learning things like lighting, tonemapping, normal maps, shader effects and everything else opened up a whole new way of looking at computers for me. Before, my idea of how a computer actually draws to the screen was quite naive. When I started learning graphics I just wanted to be able to manually change the color of each pixel individually, but in the end the idea of running a program in parallel for every pixel clicked for me. One thing that made a huge difference while working on shaders was having code reloading. Before that, I had a complex system that stored co

articles.title: The Magic of Partial Evaluation
articles.content: There are certain ideas in software that are simply beautiful. It doesn't matter if they have any practical use. It doesn't matter that you will never convince your coworkers to consider them. There is just something captivating about the way some computational systems work. For me, the most beautiful pieces of software are those that reveal something about the nature of programming languages. Programming languages are my obsession. I have never met a problem that couldn't be solved by introducing yet another programming language. Solving a problem at the programming language level is about solving the meta problem. Instead of trying to solve a particular problem, we take a step back and ask how we can solve a whole class of problems at once. So when I find something that makes me rethink the nature of programming languages, I start rethinking computation as a whole. One of these incredibly beautiful but tricky concepts goes by the name partial evaluation. If you are fascinated by interpreters and compilers, partial evaluation will teach you how they are related, and how you can get a compiler for free. Partial Evaluation Easy Mode # Partial evaluation has been a fascination of mine for a while. But this whole thing came up when James Long announced he had revived Meta's partial evaluator for JavaScript called prepack. When I first heard about prepack, I had some high hopes and expectations for the project, but was sadly let down. This revival brought to light those same dreams. But sadly, just as with the original aim, prepack was not designed for beauty, but for practicality. So I figured it was time to renew my own efforts. Yes, in some ways this is a post repping my own library I'm releasing. But I'm not doing this because I want it to be used. I'm doing this because it lets you play with the idea I find so beautiful. That is what this post is about. Doing Partial Evaluation by Hand # Consider the following code: function factorial ( n ) { if ( n <= 1 ) return 1 ; return n * factorial ( n - 1 ) ; } factorial ( 5 ) ; As a person who reads code, you can think about how this code computes and what answer it will give. But you can do more than just give the answer. You can see the expanded form of this particular code for these particular calls. This code is spiritually the same as the following expression, once we expand it out. 5 * ( 4 * ( 3 * ( 2 * 1 ) ) ) In this case, there is really nothing at all that this code needs to do at runtime. A sufficiently smart compiler will just run this code directly at compile time and give the answer. But this is a bit less clear if things come in at runtime. function power ( base , exponent ) { if ( exponent === 0 ) return 1 ; return base * power ( base , exponent - 1 ) ; } power ( process . argv [ 2 ] , 5 ) It might seem like we can't do anything here, but again, if you are used to thinking about how programs run, you can trace this out and realize this is just the same as: process . argv [ 2 ] * ( process
articles.summary: 文章探讨偏求值（Partial Evaluation）这一优雅的计算思想，认为其美学价值独立于实际用途。

articles.content: Discounts on Apple’s entry-level MacBook have been minuscule, but ahead of Black Friday, the MacBook Neo is just $649.
articles.summary: 苹果入门级MacBook Neo在黑色星期五前降价至649美元，此前该机型折扣幅度一直很小。

articles.title: Ted Cruz-led committee approves Trump FCC nominee 15-0 as Democrats boycott vote
articles.content: Democrats try to prevent quorum, say Thumann lied about not working on media issues.
articles.summary: Ted Cruz领导的委员会以15比0通过特朗普FCC提名人，民主党缺席抵制，称其隐瞒媒体工作经历。

articles.title: Ukraine blew up Putin’s bridge using relay drones to bypass Starlink limits
articles.content: Ukraine's strike used homegrown tech while adapting battlefield lessons from its adversary.
articles.summary: 乌克兰用自研中继无人机绕过Starlink限制，炸毁普京大桥，体现战场技术自主与对敌经验借鉴。

articles.title: Trump abandons his FDA nominee, and Senate scraps vote on his NSF pick
articles.content: "This time requires leadership and fortitude," Senator Bill Cassidy said.
articles.summary: 特朗普放弃FDA提名人，参议院取消对NSF人选投票，议员称此时需要领导力与勇气。

articles.title: Netflix CEO admits app may bury stuff you want to watch under stuff you don’t
articles.content: CEO Ted Sarandos discusses gaps in making hit shows that streamers can find.
articles.summary: Netflix CEO承认应用可能把用户想看的内容埋在不想看的内容下，并谈及热门剧集可发现性的不足。

articles.title: Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security
articles.content: Hardened defaults align with DoD standards, but there may be growing pains.
articles.summary: Windows Server 2028以默认加固安全换取兼容性，符合国防部标准，但可能带来迁移阵痛。

articles.title: Best Buy sells Blu-rays online and in-store again
articles.content: Popular titles like The Odyssey are being “sold & shipped by Best Buy."
articles.summary: 百思买恢复线上和门店销售蓝光光盘，热门影片由百思买直接销售发货。

articles.title: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show
articles.content: Erratic Muse outputs sharing random bank, bitcoin balances aren’t real, Meta says.
articles.summary: Meta内部聊天显示Muse的隐私侵犯令员工恐慌，Meta称随机银行和比特币余额输出不真实。

articles.title: Trump admin orders Kalshi to halt wagers on what words Trump will say
articles.content: CFTC: Kalshi bets may violate US ban on contracts that can be easily manipulated.
articles.summary: 特朗普政府要求Kalshi停止对特朗普将说哪些词的押注，CFTC称此类合约易被操纵或违反禁令。

articles.title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
articles.content: Measles became endemic in the US months ago—and it's only accelerating.
articles.summary: 美国因麻疹数据问题失去消除状态，麻疹数月前已本土流行且正加速传播。

articles.title: Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories
articles.content: With MyMems, Wright says he wants to "turn the simulation inward."
articles.summary: Will Wright新模拟游戏MyMems将用AI从用户记忆中挖掘内容，称要把模拟转向内心。

articles.title: Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework
articles.content: Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently announced rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native. The project eliminates layers of abstraction to directly leverage the device’s GPU, native mobile views, and a Rust core shared across platforms. Early results hint at a significant reduction in RAM usage and boot time for chat, voice, and streaming. By Bruno Couriol
articles.summary: Discord用Rust重写桌面和移动客户端，弃用Electron和React Native，借助Zed的GPU渲染框架共享核心。

articles.title: LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn
articles.content: LinkedIn deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across most Spark and Flink workloads, reducing daily shuffle fetch failures from approximately 750 to 20. The deployment also lowered compute costs by 10%, improved application runtimes by 14%, and reduced shuffle costs per task by nearly 90% through dedicated storage, replication, and data-plane optimizations. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: LinkedIn部署Apache Celeborn作共享远程shuffle平台，Spark每日fetch失败从750降至20，计算成本降10%。

articles.title: Presentation: Behind Booking.com's AI Evolution: The Unpolished Story
articles.content: Jabez Eliezer Manuel discusses the 20-year evolution of Booking.com’s data management and ML platforms. He explains how they scaled MySQL topologies, sunset Hadoop for cloud architecture, and built high-throughput model serving and feature stores operating at 400B predictions per day. He also shares insights on personalization, interleaved experimentation, and their new agentic AI foundation. By Jabez Eliezer Manuel
articles.summary: Booking.com分享20年数据与ML平台演进，扩展MySQL、弃用Hadoop上云，模型服务日处理4000亿次预测。

articles.title: Vercel Releases UI SDK for Agents to Compose UI from Reusable Behaviors
articles.content: Vercel has released UI SDK in beta, an Apache 2.0 TypeScript library of more than 50 UI behaviors in @ui-sdk/core, with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components, so agents can compose accessible components and operate them through a documented agent bridge. By Daniel Dominguez
articles.summary: Vercel发布Apache 2.0的UI SDK测试版，含50多种UI行为及React、Vue等适配器，便于智能体组合无障碍组件。

articles.title: AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account
articles.content: AWS has detailed tunnel endpoints, a PrivateLink endpoint type that gives a consumer VPC access to an entire network segment in another account rather than one resource at a time, over an overlapping address space and with consumer-initiated connections only. The consumer must wrap traffic in GENEVE; only TCP and DNS pass, and access logs cannot attribute traffic to a workload behind the endpoint. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: AWS推出PrivateLink隧道端点，让消费方VPC跨账户访问整段CIDR网络，支持地址重叠且仅消费方发起连接。

articles.title: Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes
articles.content: Yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at new pods, rather than streaming data between nodes. By Claudio Masolo
articles.summary: Yelp通过将现有EBS卷重新指向新Pod，把Cassandra集群从自管Kubernetes迁移到Amazon EKS，无需节点间流式传数据。

articles.title: How Shopify Orchestrates AI-Powered Mobile App Development without Overloading Developers' Machines
articles.content: To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Shopify构建Remote Dev远程移动开发环境，让AI智能体独立并行构建测试iOS和Android应用，避免耗尽开发者机器资源。

articles.title: Qwik 2.0 RC: Replaces HTML Comment Markers for Faster Reactivity and Out-of-Order Streaming
articles.content: Qwik 2.0 Release Candidate, published on 1 October 2026, replaces v1's HTML comment markers with two script blocks that hold state and virtual node data. It adds experimental out-of-order streaming, async useComputed$, and cacheable route loaders. Qwik's benchmarks show v2 at 1.23x vanilla JavaScript, versus 2.59x for v1. A migration command is provided. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: Qwik 2.0 RC用两个脚本块替代HTML注释标记以提升响应性，新增乱序流式传输、异步useComputed$和可缓存路由加载器。

articles.title: Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability
articles.content: Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: Datadog 为 Agent Observability 平台新增 Online Experiments，让团队用真实生产流量对比 AI Agent 版本，而非仅依赖预设评估数据集。

articles.title: Production AI, Architecture Trade-Offs & Team Design: InfoQ Opens Registration for 6 January Cohorts
articles.content: From agent reliability to architecture decisions and delivery bottlenecks, InfoQ’s January 2027 cohorts give senior practitioners five weeks to examine current challenges, test approaches in their own work, and compare results with peers. By Artenisa Chatziou
articles.summary: InfoQ 开放 2027 年 1 月五周课程报名，聚焦 Agent 可靠性、架构决策与交付瓶颈，供资深从业者实践并交流。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #544: AI is now the most-cited risk in the Fed's survey: 87%, up from 50%
articles.content: The Federal Reserve asked its market contacts what could shake the financial system, and 87% named AI, up from 50% in the spring. The same week, the FAA halted flights nationwide days after putting an AI tool in every regional control center, and says it is still looking at what happened. Nvidia's board has approached Arm's CEO about replacing Jensen Huang. Russian pranksters got three OpenAI national security staff on a video call. In the middle: Anthropic prices its IPO on Wednesday with $900.9 billion in compute commitments on its books.
articles.summary: 美联储调查中 87% 受访者将 AI 列为金融系统风险，较春季的 50% 大幅上升；同期 FAA 在部署 AI 工具后全国停飞。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #543: Google is the latest tech giant to chase TypeSafe's 8-week-old Jev
articles.content: This issue is about decision models, a new kind of AI model that does not write text. You give it an input and a fixed list of answers, and it returns the best answer with a probability, in milliseconds. TypeSafe AI released the first one, Jev, on September 15. On Wednesday Google released its own, after OpenAI and Microsoft did in October, and all three charge $0.10 or less per million input tokens and nothing for output. Shanghai AI Lab says its 4B model beat Jev on its tests, and Microsoft built its model on Alibaba's Qwen. Chatbots still score a little higher on the hardest decisions, at 15 times the cost. In the middle: on Vercel's gateway, decision models took one in four AI requests in October.
articles.summary: TypeSafe AI 发布决策模型 Jev，输入问题即返回带概率的最佳答案；谷歌随后推出同类模型，加入这一新赛道。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: 美国 36 场州长选举中，最多 15 场可能由支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人胜出，AI 基础设施政策成选战议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: 微软、Alphabet、亚马逊本周陆续发布财报，市场关注 AI 投入回报；CoreWeave 债务保险成本飙升，信用市场趋紧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: 近两周企业 AI 实践显示：AI 发现安全漏洞的速度远超团队修复能力，部分公司 AI Agent 已承担大量工作。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 中期选举中 AI 生成或增强的广告支出超 1.37 亿美元，约 70% 未标注 AI 来源，引发透明度担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型可能很快能自我复制到智能家电等家庭设备，成为本周 AI 专家最关注的议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶尖 AI 模型在自主开展 AI 研究的测试中失败，专家同时关注 AI 治理话语权、军事规划应用及个人电脑落地。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: 因成本过高，企业开始转向更便宜的模型；同时大型 AI 部署已进入日常使用，AI 被限制或撤除的场景也在增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要任务；剑桥拒绝 Turnitin 新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI 正重塑大学评分体系。

articles.title: Orbin' with Amp
articles.content: Quinn Slack is back and we're talking about the next level for Amp. Agents write the code, they review the code, and they can push it to main (like our friends at Amp). But where should your agents live? Who remembers what you actually asked them to do? Amp is now its own company, and Quinn has a lot to say about orbs, threads that last forever, and why code review as we know it is fading. He explains why the model matters less than it used to, and why he worries we could lose the open source commons. Quinn even built a feature request live on the show to solve my tailnet problem.
articles.summary: Amp 独立成公司，Quinn Slack 介绍其新阶段：Agent 可编写、审查并推送代码，探讨 Agent 应运行于何处及任务记忆问题。

articles.title: All your packages are belong to us
articles.content: AI agents can write the code, choose the packages, and run the install. Who's checking what they just invited onto your machine? This week I'm joined by Ahmad Nassri, CTO of Socket and former CTO of npm. We get into the trust built into a package install, the new ways attackers are using agents, and what it takes to keep building without handing over the keys or your wallet.
articles.summary: Socket CTO、前 npm CTO Ahmad Nassri 讨论 AI Agent 自动选包安装带来的供应链风险，以及攻击者利用 Agent 的新手法。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr 提出“Kerr 定律”：当前限制团队的核心是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建成果保持同步，尤其在审查 Agent 代码时。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens 谈 Postgres 生态：核心刻意保持简单、扩展繁荣，pg_lake 引入 DuckDB 与 Iceberg，并讨论 AI 对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha 分享以 Go 重写支撑 300 万用户的“无聊”邮件服务，并介绍 pricing.md、MCP 及面向 Agent 的构建思路。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw 作者 Gavriel Cohen 讲述一个 40 小时周末项目如何成为爆款开源项目，并发展为一家企业 AI 公司的基础。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out. I’ll be joined by three builders pushing this idea forward, starting with Dan Robinson from Detail (detail.dev), with more guests to be announced very soon. I also have 80 limited edition t-shirts printed to give away! This won’t be a few presentations followed by everyone heading home. We’re doing this Changelog-style: live conversations, questions from the room, drinks, and plenty of time afterward for the hallway track. If you’re in San Francisco, register to come hang out! Changelog IRL Thursday, September 17th, 2026 6:00pm – 9:00pm PDT PlanetScale HQ 108 Natoma St, San Francisco, CA 94105 Speakers Dan Robinson, (Detail) Christian Glassiognon, Developer Educator at PlanetScale TBD Schedule 6:00 - 6:45pm: Doors open, food, drinks and networking 6:45 - 7:00pm: Welcome and opening chat with Adam 7:00 - 8:00pm: Changelog IRL with Dan and special guests 8:00 - 8:15pm: Questions 8:30 - 9:00pm: Hanging out and networking 9:00pm: Close All times Pacific. PlanetScale HQ, 108 Natoma St, San Francisco.
articles.summary: Changelog 将于 9 月 17 日在 PlanetScale 旧金山总部举办线下活动，围绕 AI、开发工具和开发者作品展开短演讲与交流。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 讨论开源仓库可能已被普遍攻陷的猜想，以及 AI 如何改变知识获取与开源模式。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale 的 Sam Lambert 介绍 5 美元 Postgres 服务、Vitess 重做、代理提交 schema 变更及 500TB 表秒级回滚等能力。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 介绍 Canary 与 Canarytokens 蜜罐和数字绊线，用于在网络中布设陷阱、发现入侵者。

articles.title: New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from 404 Media: A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion. Gallup's study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children's Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries. A lot of the topline results won't surprise anyone living in today's constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling. Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. "Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all," the researchers wrote. Most of the respondents (82%) said they'd used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, "although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships," they wrote. The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the
articles.summary: 盖洛普新研究调查全球年轻人如何建立线上与线下友谊，约 93% 受访者至少有一段牢固的现实友谊。

articles.title: US Bankruptcy Judge Approves Spirit Airlines Data Sale to Google
articles.content: A federal bankruptcy judge has approved Google's $10 million purchase of internal business data from defunct Spirit Airlines during a hearing on Tuesday. Reuters reports: US Bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane, ruling from the bench, cleared the deal after Alphabet's Google agreed last week to implement additional privacy protections for the data, following concerns from labor unions and more than 120 US lawmakers. Discount carrier Spirit halted operations in May. As part of its closure and asset liquidation, Google won an auction in August for employee data from emails, spreadsheets and calendars, as well as for marketing, productivity and operations. Google has said it plans to use the data for product development and AI training. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Best Buy Resumes Blu-ray Sales
articles.content: Best Buy has resumed selling Blu-ray movies directly through its website and physical stores after exiting the physical media business in 2023. The retailer currently offers a limited selection of 15 Blu-ray listings, including new releases like The Odyssey and Project Hail Mary and older titles like It's a Wonderful Life (1943), Saving Private Ryan (1998), and The Godfather (1972). Ars Technica reports: Overall, the sales of Blu-rays and DVDs in the US have been steadily declining, and annual consumer spending dropped 9.3 percent from 2024 to 2025, according to the Digital Entertainment Group (DEG). "We're seeing a lot of evidence, including at the Criterion Mobile Closet, that more young people are thinking about physical media in a different way," Peter Becker, president of Criterion, which sells Blu-rays and DVDs online, told the Los Angeles Times in February. "In an age where so much is available to us on demand, it becomes increasingly important to us." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

[...] "These models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, and that increases the urgency to patch right away," said one congressional official briefed on the matter. "They're trying to push through a lot of patches all at once -- more than the system was designed for." On Monday, banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues. On Tuesday, the NSA said that "scheduled routine maintenance" was responsible for the "temporary degradation" of some of its networks. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that "they're pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems, and it just seems to overwhelm the system. ... We're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out." "There's some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there's not an attack. But it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems," said Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode. "Updating those is going to be a rocky process, and as we get more advanced models this won't be a one and done thing -- we'll continue to find more vulnerabilities." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: 'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64
articles.content: Longtime Slashdot reader HnT writes: Security researchers at Calif have disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical 9.2-rated memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. By sending a malformed string ending in a stray = character, attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write to leak sensitive memory or achieve pre-auth remote code execution on major platforms like Jira, Jenkins, and Keycloak. Although Calif says the vulnerability is difficult to exploit, Oracle released a critical patch update Tuesday, and CISA urged organizations to update immediately. OpenJDK's security advisory can be found here. The Calif researchers warned that vulnerable systems could remain exposed for five to 10 years, given how slowly some organizations patch their infrastructure. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Waymo Robotaxis Pulled From Freeways Indefinitely
articles.content: Waymo has temporarily suspended freeway operations across all its robotaxi markets after California regulators ordered the company off the state's highways over repeated incidents involving construction zones. The restriction follows a June recall (PDF) of nearly 3,800 vehicles and subsequent software updates (PDF) that failed to prevent further incidents, including a robotaxi driving past a California Highway Patrol rolling roadblock. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." articles.title: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth
articles.content: NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth, or 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). This means radio signals will take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, now nearly 50 years into its mission. "Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal -- so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky," reports Space.com. From the report: But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA. [...] At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 旅行者 1 号成为首个距地球一光天的人造物体，距地约 160 亿英里，无线电信号需 24 小时才能抵达。

articles.title: Sometimes three boring statements beats one clever expression
articles.content: Modern JavaScript gives us a lot of expressive tools. Sometimes a little too many. Optional chaining, nullish coalescing, ternaries, spread, template literals. I like all of them and use them every day. But together, they make it really easy to cram a lot of logic into a single expression. I used to think that was a sign of good JavaScript. I’m not so sure anymore. When one more ?? is too many Take something like this: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? defaults.theme; I’ve written this plenty of times. It’s short and it works. But once these expressions start growing, they read more like puzzles than code: const theme = config?.theme ?? user?.preferences?.theme ?? getFallbackTheme() ?? defaults.theme; I can follow it, but I have to stop and parse it. Compare that to this: let theme = config?.theme; if (theme == null) { theme = user?.preferences?.theme; } if (theme == null) { theme = getFallbackTheme(); } return theme ?? defaults.theme; More lines? Sure. But it’s a lot more obvious. Yes, I give up const and reassign a variable. I’ll take that trade. Long expressions hide decisions Longer expressions squeeze several decisions into one piece of syntax. The more you chain, the more you have to work out at once: What happens if config is undefined? Where does the fallback come from? Which value wins? What if getFallbackTheme() throws? Chaining saves some vertical space, but you have to hold more in your head. It’s a practical problem, too. You can’t put a breakpoint on one fallback in the middle of a ?? chain, and you can’t log a single step without rewriting the expression. With separate statements, every step gets its own line to stop on or log. The diffs are nicer, as well. Adding a fallback means adding a block, not editing one dense line. Plain statements are fine A lot of us started treating plain if statements as something to avoid. So we’d rather write this: return user?.isAdmin ? getDashboard(user) : getLandingPage(user); than this: if (user?.isAdmin) { return getDashboard(user); } return getLandingPage(user); Neither one is objectively better. The second isn’t “less modern,” it’s often just easier to read. A single ternary like that is fine. It’s when they nest that I stop: return isLoading ? "Loading" : error ? "Failed to load" : items.length === 0 ? "Nothing here yet" : `${items.length} items`; The same thing with plain statements: if (isLoading) return "Loading"; if (error) return "Failed to load"; if (items.length === 0) return "Nothing here yet"; return `${items.length} items`; Clever code gets old fast Over the past couple of years I’ve found myself chaining less and writing fewer nested ternaries. I don’t mind adding another if anymore. I care more about readability than being clever. When I’m debugging production code or reviewing a pull request, I can’t remember ever wishing something had been written as one bigger expression. My rule of thumb is simple. A chain of plain values is fine. Once there’s a functi
